nameStory: The "shaggy soldier" gets its common name from its fuzzy, hairy appearance that gives it a somewhat disheveled look, like a soldier who's been through a long campaign. The tiny white flowers with their short petals might remind you of a raggedy uniform, while the plant's ability to colonize disturbed ground mirrors how soldiers move into new territory.
description: Shaggy soldier is a small, weedy annual flower that rarely grows taller than your knee. It produces tiny daisy-like flowers with four or five short white petals surrounding a yellow center, each flower only about the size of your pinky nail. The entire plant has a soft, fuzzy texture due to fine hairs covering the stems and leaves. Originally from Mexico, this little survivor has made itself at home in gardens, sidewalk cracks, and waste places throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white daisy-like flowers, each smaller than a dime, with 4-5 very short white petals around a yellow center. The petals are so short they're almost square-shaped, and flowers bloom continuously from summer through fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing, branching annual that forms small bushy clumps. The whole plant feels soft and slightly fuzzy when you brush against it, rarely growing taller than 2 feet.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval-shaped leaves that taper to a point, arranged in pairs along the stem (opposite arrangement). The leaves feel soft and slightly hairy, with visible veins running from base to tip.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark seeds topped with tiny white bristles that help them catch the wind. Seeds are produced abundantly and scatter easily when the plant is disturbed.

habitat: Shaggy soldier thrives in disturbed soils and human-modified landscapes throughout New England. Look for it in vegetable gardens, flower beds, along sidewalks, in vacant lots, and anywhere the soil has been recently turned or disturbed. It particularly loves rich, moist soil but tolerates a wide range of conditions from full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of fuzzy oval leaves. Early plants may begin flowering by late spring in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with continuous production of tiny white flowers. Plants branch out and spread, producing seeds that germinate quickly to create new plants.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering until first hard frost. Seeds mature and scatter, with late-season plants often producing the most abundant seed crops.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely with frost, leaving no above-ground parts. Seeds overwinter in the soil to germinate next growing season.

funFact: A single shaggy soldier plant can produce over 7,000 seeds in one growing season, and those seeds can germinate and grow into flowering plants in just 6-8 weeks, meaning you could theoretically have three generations of shaggy soldiers in one New England summer!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its close relative gallant soldier, but shaggy soldier lives up to its name by being noticeably more hairy and fuzzy all over. Memory trick: "Shaggy soldiers need a shave" - if the plant feels soft and fuzzy when you touch it, it's the shaggy one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Peruvian daisy" in some regions, shaggy soldier actually originates from Mexico, not Peru. The scientific name honors Spanish botanist Mariano Martínez de Galinsoga, showing how plant names can honor people even when common names point to the wrong countries.
compareHints: Shaggy soldier differs from its close relative gallant soldier primarily in its hairiness - shaggy soldier is noticeably more fuzzy throughout, while gallant soldier is nearly smooth. The flower petals on shaggy soldier are also typically a bit more prominent, though both species have the characteristic tiny white daisy-like blooms with yellow centers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Gallant soldier differs from its close relative shaggy soldier primarily in its smooth, hairless stems and leaves, while shaggy soldier is distinctly fuzzy and hairy throughout.
